title: Leave a system someone can own
standfirst: Delivery includes the evidence, decisions and recovery paths that survive the original builder.

blocks.text: A production system outlives the run that made it look successful. Sources change, models are replaced, users ask for adjacent things, and someone inherits an exception the original builder understood without writing down. The final architectural question is who can recognize that the system’s promise has changed—and what they are able to do about it.

Sculley and colleagues’ Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems describes dependencies that escape the apparent model boundary: data changes, undeclared consumers and feedback loops can couple systems that look separate in code. An AI production pipeline inherits that problem whenever another process begins relying on its output. Shipping creates a relationship to maintain, even if the generating code remains untouched.

Return to our hypothetical weekly research brief after release. A sales team starts copying its “ready” findings into customer messages. Then a source changes its date field, and old material is presented as new. The brief still arrives on time. Its consumer has acquired a dependence the original evaluation did not cover. The problem now belongs to the production system, even if the model’s prose remains excellent.
Release a selection, not the newest directory

blocks.title: What went into the box
blocks.caption: These are recorded selection boundaries, not three grades averaged into one. Keeping a failed result with the release lets the next owner choose a different commission without rewriting this one.

blocks.text: Loopforge’s delivery is useful here as a selection problem. An accepted control correction shipped; a newer rescue solver did not. The experiment remained available to inspect, while the playable package retained its existing behavior. The failed device result remained a failure beside the release. These distinctions let a recipient know what was chosen, what was attempted and what had not been established.

There is real loss in that decision. The effort spent on the solver cannot be recovered by installing it, and preserving it does not make its contact failures disappear. But deleting the experiment would throw away something different: the next animator’s chance to inspect why it failed. A handoff can protect both the playable result and the unsuccessful inquiry, provided their status is impossible to confuse.

A production handoff needs the same distinctions for prompts, models, source data, tool contracts and evaluation rules. Identify the combination that was tested. Preserve a return path to a known usable version where one exists. If a later change improves one task but breaks another consumer, the operator needs more than the assurance that the latest candidate scored better.

A rollback also has a boundary. Reverting a prompt does not undo an email already sent or a record already changed. The release plan must say which effects are reversible, which need compensation and who owns the unresolved result. This is where the execution contracts from the beginning of the book become obligations to another person.

In that example, the operator pauses publication, identifies the affected source snapshot and extractor configuration, and restores a known interpretation or holds the next issue for review. Already-sent claims still need correction. The handoff must therefore name both a technical owner and someone responsible for the receiving team. Reverting code alone cannot recall a customer message.
Choose the next intervention

Boris Tane describes a revealing plan annotation: an existing queue consumer already owns retries, so the proposed change should not add another retry layer. The written plan gives the owner a place to inject knowledge the agent’s local solution omitted. Here, planning is valuable because it prevents duplicated responsibility before more code depends on it.

A movement problem may require the opposite timing. Peter Steinberger’s account allows the idea to change after a working version can be inspected. Loopforge’s rescue needed a visible interval as well as protected state obligations. I had helped create a process that could always find and assign another defect. Closing the package forced a different judgment: a true criticism could justify a future commission without automatically delaying this one.

Hashimoto’s adoption account offers a third use of effort: repeating work with an agent to discover where the surrounding tools and instructions fail, then choosing bounded unattended work that can leave a useful next-day starting point. The investment is in a better future process. Its output is not automatically a shipped result. That distinction keeps a successful experiment from becoming an unearned delivery claim.
Measure the work the recipient inherits

blocks.title: The account with a missing edge
blocks.caption: The largest field is cache reuse. Its size gives us a question about recurring context; it cannot tell us which repeated input was necessary, or what the finished day was worth.

blocks.text: The studio’s resource ledger is striking and incomplete. Its reported interval contains extensive cached input alongside other model activity; it excludes parts of coordination and supplies no complete billed-dollar total. Dividing it by the game’s fictional output count would create a ratio without a useful unit. The ledger can describe observed use, but it cannot establish the economic value of the delivered software.

Forsgren describes reports that counted executed tests and closed bugs while overlooking work that helped systems ship and remain online. Her account of SPACE asks for several dimensions of developer productivity. The mismatch is present in our ledger without any elaborate calculation. We can identify observed machine activity much more precisely than we can say what the selected correction was worth.

For the brief’s date error, the immediate choice is to correct this issue by hand or build a source-contract check that can guard future issues. Keep the acceptance standard fixed. The reusable check needs implementation, review and maintenance; manual checking consumes attention every run. If the brief will serve many future issues with the same contract, that repeated saving may repay the setup. For a one-off report, or a source about to be replaced, the smaller manual repair may be the better purchase.

The comparison must also include what the check misses. A valid date field can still contain misleading material; keeping a human review at the consequential claim may remain worthwhile. Record one-time adoption separately from recurring model, tool, review and repair work over a useful horizon. The ledger cannot make that decision for us. It helps only after the result and the alternatives have been defined.
Leave a decision the successor can make

blocks.title: A brief that can come back with a decision
blocks.caption: Choose a bounded investigation or the continuing research-brief service. The eight editable sections include ownership, change triggers and recovery. A completed sheet is a proposed agreement, not permission to act.

blocks.text: The editable sheet includes a continuing-service example for the research brief. It names the source contract, the publication hold, the owner of affected communications and the evidence needed to resume. The factory examples remain useful for bounded investigations. Their different scopes prevent a one-time repair from silently becoming an open-ended operating responsibility.

The successor’s first hour is a useful measure of the package. There is a specimen to open, an observation to reproduce, obligations to preserve and a decision to bring back. A failed attempt belongs on that path if it changes what the successor should try. A long transcript may remain behind a source link when a short account of the failure does the immediate work. Preserving everything in the same foreground can make the useful beginning disappear.

The stopping line is where the sheet becomes difficult. “Improve until good” lets every discovery enlarge the assignment. “Return one measured repair, or the evidence that the proposed cause was wrong” permits a failed repair to finish a useful piece of work. The owner receives a new fact instead of another obligation disguised as progress. That is a smaller promise, and one whose fulfillment can finally be recognized.

The handoff is tested when a successor can reproduce that failure and make the next decision without the original builder interpreting every record. One source change is enough to rehearse the path: notice the broken promise, stop the affected publication, identify what escaped and return with evidence for resuming. A long archive is useful behind that path; it should not be the path.

blocks.title: Run one bounded commission
blocks.body: Use the downloadable protocol with the editable sheet. It works for a generated asset, a data pipeline, a game action or a browser feature; the receiving evidence must change with the job.
steps: Choose one recipient and one useful difference. Pin the starting result and the obligations that must survive.
Give the implementer a complete small slice and access to the observation that can reject it. Separate work only where the receiving boundary is explicit.
Inspect the exact returned specimen. Record repair, acceptance, deferral or stop together with the reason and remaining resource allowance.
Hand over the runnable result, evidence and unresolved findings. A successor gets a new commission; a failed check does not silently restart the old one.
blocks.exercise: Take one unfinished item from your own work. Write the smallest investigation that could make you decide against continuing it. If no possible result would change your decision, reconsider what the investigation is for.

blocks.text: The rescue experiment could remain available without remaining an instruction. That was the decision I had to learn to make: preserve the finding, select the usable work, and leave a successor the authority to choose a different next attempt. A production system deserves the same clarity after every release. Someone should be able to tell what it promises, what changed and where to intervene—without reconstructing the studio that built it.
